title: The change control process
blurb: Put the six change control stages in order and follow a real request through every one.
question: On a new medical centre build, the GP partners ask for an extra consulting room after the design is baselined. What are the stages this request must pass through, in order, before the builders start work?

teach.h: Six stages, always in this order
teach.body: A typical change control process has six stages: change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans, implement. The order is the point. You screen a request quickly before spending effort on it, you understand the full impact before deciding, and you update the plans before anyone starts work. The exam tests both the names and the sequence.

steps.label: Change request
steps.sub: Raised and logged in the change log

steps.label: Initial evaluation
steps.sub: Quick look: is it worth a full assessment?

steps.label: Detailed evaluation
steps.sub: Impact on scope, time, cost, quality, risk, benefits

steps.label: Recommendation
steps.sub: Approve, reject or defer; the sponsor or authority decides

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: Make the change and communicate it

teach.caption: APM BoK 7th edition sequence. Learn it as a chain: each stage feeds the next.

teach.h: Real Investors Do Research, Update, Invest
teach.word: R I D R U I
teach.caption: Initial comes before Detailed (small look, then big look). Update comes before Implement (change the plan, then the work).

teach.body: Westbrook Medical Centre is a new-build GP surgery. The design and budget were baselined in definition. Two months into construction, the GP partners ask for an extra consulting room to cope with a growing patient list. The project manager does not tell the builder to go ahead. Instead, the request becomes CR-014 and enters change control. Follow it through all six stages below.

head: Stage
What happens at Westbrook
rows: Partners ask for an extra room; PM logs CR-014
PM: fits the objectives; worth a full look
Architect and QS: about +£45k, +3 weeks, redesign, more appointments
Baseline, schedule, budget, PMP and drawings to rev C
Builder instructed, staff told, CR-014 closed
teach.caption: Figures are illustrative. Notice nothing is built until stage 6.

rows.label: Looks at
values: Scope, time, cost, quality, risk, benefits

teach.caption: The two evaluations are separate stages: the quick screen protects the team from wasting effort on unrealistic requests.

root.label: Recommendation
root.sub: PM recommends; sponsor or appropriate authority decides

teach.caption: Only an approved change moves on to stages 5 and 6. Every decision is recorded in the change log.

teach.body: Once CR-014 is approved, the baseline, schedule, budget, project management plan and configuration records are updated first. Then the work is measured against the new baseline, and the builder works from drawing rev C, not rev B. Implementation then makes the change and communicates it to everyone affected. Swap these two stages and people build from plans that no longer match the decision.

teach.text: 'Justification', 'Planning' and 'Continuous improvement' are NOT change control stages, however sensible they sound. Watch the order traps too: detailed evaluation never comes before initial evaluation, and implement never comes before update plans.

items: Six stages in order: change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans, implement.
Initial evaluation is a quick screen; detailed evaluation assesses impact on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits.
At recommendation the change is approved, rejected or deferred by the sponsor or appropriate authority.
Plans, baseline and configuration records are updated before the change is implemented and communicated.

summary: You can now list the six change control stages in the correct order and say what happens at each. You can also follow a single change request from being raised to being implemented, and reject the classic distractor stages.

A.q: What is the first stage of a typical change control process?
A.why: Everything starts with a change request being raised and logged.

whyNot.0: Initial evaluation is the second stage: there must be a request to evaluate first.
whyNot.2: Recommendation is the fourth stage, after both evaluations.
whyNot.3: Detailed evaluation is the third stage, after the initial screen.

A.q: In a typical change control process, which stage immediately follows initial evaluation?
A.why: After the quick initial screen, a worthwhile request receives a detailed evaluation of its impact.

whyNot.0: Recommendation comes after detailed evaluation, once the impact is understood.
whyNot.1: Plans are only updated after a change has been approved.
whyNot.2: The change request is the first stage, before initial evaluation.

A.q: At which stage is a decision made to approve, reject or defer a change?
A.why: At the recommendation stage the change is approved, rejected or deferred by the sponsor or appropriate authority.

whyNot.1: Initial evaluation only decides whether a full assessment is worthwhile.
whyNot.2: Plans are updated after the decision to approve has been made.
whyNot.3: At the change request stage the request is only raised and logged.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a stage in a typical change control process?
B.why: Continuous improvement belongs to quality management. It is not a change control stage.

B.q: Which list shows the last three change control stages in the correct order?
B.why: The decision comes first, then the plans are updated, then the change is implemented.

whyNot.0: Implementing before updating the plans means people work from out-of-date plans.
whyNot.1: Plans cannot be updated before the change has been approved.
whyNot.3: This reverses the whole sequence: nothing should be implemented before a decision.

B.q: During the detailed evaluation of Westbrook's CR-014, what does the team mainly assess?
options: Who first suggested the extra room
The impact on time, cost, quality and risk
Which supplier offers the cheapest price
How the change will be announced to staff
B.why: Detailed evaluation assesses the full impact of the change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits.

whyNot.0: Who raised it is recorded at the change request stage; it is not what is being evaluated.
whyNot.2: Supplier pricing may feed the cost estimate, but it is not the purpose of the evaluation.
whyNot.3: Communicating the change happens at implementation, after approval.

C.q: Westbrook's sponsor has approved CR-014. The site manager wants the builders to start today, before any plans are revised. What does the change control process require?
options: Start now and update the plans at handover
Re-run the initial evaluation of the room
Update the baseline and plans, then build
Raise a fresh change request for the room
C.why: After the decision comes update plans, then implement: the baseline, plans and configuration records change before the work does.

whyNot.0: Building first leaves everyone working against plans that no longer match the decision.
whyNot.1: The evaluations are already complete; repeating them adds nothing.
whyNot.3: The request has already been raised and approved; a new one is not needed.

C.q: A change request is logged. The PM's quick review finds it clashes with the project's objectives, so no full assessment is carried out. Which stage was this?
C.why: Initial evaluation is the quick screen that decides whether a request is worth a full assessment.

whyNot.1: Detailed evaluation is the full assessment, which never took place here.
whyNot.2: Recommendation follows the evaluations and leads to the formal decision.
whyNot.3: Implement is the final stage, for approved changes only.

C.q: Which THREE of these are stages in a typical change control process? 1. Justification 2. Initial evaluation 3. Update plans 4. Implement
C.why: Initial evaluation (2), update plans (3) and implement (4) are all stages. Justification is not.

whyNot.0: Justification (1) is a distractor, not a change control stage.
whyNot.1: Justification (1) is a distractor, not a change control stage.
whyNot.2: Justification (1) is a distractor, not a change control stage.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: Your new kitchen is agreed and the fitters have started. You suddenly want an island instead of a peninsula. What should happen before anyone moves a cabinet?

blocks.h: The same six stages at home
blocks.body: You ask the kitchen company for an island: that is the change request. The designer glances at it: is there even room? That is the initial evaluation. If yes, they work out the extra cost, the delay and the plumbing changes: the detailed evaluation. They recommend it and you agree. They redraw the plans and the order. Only then do the fitters build it.

blocks.text: If the fitters built the island before the drawings and order were updated, the wrong worktop would arrive. That is why update plans comes before implement.

explain.h: Stages 1 and 2: request and initial evaluation
explain.body: Anyone can raise a change request, and it is logged in the change log so nothing is lost. Initial evaluation is a quick screen: does the request make sense and is it worth the effort of a full assessment?

steps.label: Change request
steps.sub: Raised and logged with a reference

test.q: Where is a new change request recorded when it is raised?
test.why: Change requests are logged in the change log so each one can be tracked to a decision.

whyNot.0: The risk register records uncertain events, not requests for change.
whyNot.1: The lessons log captures learning for the future.
whyNot.2: A benefits profile describes how and when a benefit will be realised.

explain.body: A full assessment of the change's impact on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits. Specialists help, and the configuration records show which items would be affected.

test.q: What is the main purpose of the detailed evaluation stage?
options: To decide quickly if a full review is needed
To assess the full impact of the change
To tell stakeholders the change is now live
To update the baseline and the PMP
test.why: Detailed evaluation assesses the full impact of the change before any recommendation is made.

whyNot.0: The quick screen is the initial evaluation.
whyNot.2: Communicating the change is part of implementation.
whyNot.3: Updating the baseline and PMP is the update plans stage.

explain.body: Using the evaluation, the project manager recommends approve, reject or defer. The decision is made by the sponsor or whoever holds the authority for that size of change. The outcome is recorded and the requester is told.

test.q: Who normally makes the final decision on a significant change request?
options: The person who raised the request
The team member who will build it
test.why: The sponsor, or the authority set by the project's governance, decides whether the change is approved, rejected or deferred.

whyNot.0: The requester asks for the change; they do not approve their own request.
whyNot.1: The team implements approved changes; it does not authorise them.
whyNot.3: A supplier may provide estimates but has no authority over the project baseline.

explain.h: Stages 5 and 6: update plans, then implement
explain.body: An approved change first updates the baseline, the project management plan and the configuration records. Then the change is implemented and communicated to everyone affected, and the change log is closed off.

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: Do the work and communicate it

test.q: What is updated during the 'update plans' stage?
options: The baseline, PMP and configuration records
The business case template and policies
The lessons log from previous projects
test.why: Update plans revises the baseline, the project management plan and the configuration records to reflect the approved change.

whyNot.1: Strategy and portfolio are set above the project, not by a single change request.
whyNot.2: Templates and policies are organisational standards, not project plans.
whyNot.3: Lessons from previous projects are not changed by a current change request.
